task_row_model.query: What experimental conditions and measurement method did the study use to test whether intermittent fasting improves insulin sensitivity in middle-aged adults?

documents.content: In a randomized controlled trial, researchers enrolled 120 middle-aged adults (aged 40–60) with body mass index between 25 and 30 to evaluate time-restricted eating. Participants were assigned to a daily intermittent fasting regimen of 16 hours fasting and an 8-hour eating window for 12 weeks, while the control group was asked to continue their usual diet without timing restrictions. Participants were instructed to maintain their baseline caloric intake and usual physical activity throughout the study. The paper briefly notes historical fasting practices in religious and cultural traditions as background, but the trial focused on the 16:8 schedule and adherence was tracked with daily logs.

The methods section describes metabolic assessments performed at baseline and after 12 weeks. Insulin sensitivity was quantified using HOMA-IR, calculated from fasting plasma glucose and fasting insulin concentrations obtained from venous blood samples. Additionally, a standard 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) was administered with measurement of 2-hour plasma glucose to evaluate post-load glucose handling. Blood samples for fasting assays were collected after a 10–12 hour overnight fast. Laboratory insulin and glucose assays were performed by immunoassay and enzymatic methods. The authors mention QUICKI and clamp techniques in the discussion as alternative indices but did not use them in this trial.

A news-style summary highlighted participant selection and trial conduct, noting that individuals with diagnosed diabetes or on glucose-lowering medications were excluded, and that the study randomized volunteers to the time-restricted eating arm or control. The article quoted a lead investigator describing wearable devices and smartphone logs used to corroborate self-reported meal timing; it also included comparative anecdotes about alternate fasting regimens such as alternate-day fasting, which were not evaluated in this protocol. Some background statistics on population obesity trends were provided but were not part of the trial data.

task_row_model.golden_answer: The study was a 12-week randomized controlled trial in 120 middle-aged adults (40–60 years, BMI 25–30) comparing daily 16:8 intermittent fasting (16-hour fast, 8-hour eating window) to a control group maintaining their usual diet. Insulin sensitivity was measured at baseline and 12 weeks by HOMA-IR from fasting plasma glucose and insulin, and by a 75 g OGTT with 2-hour plasma glucose; fasting samples followed a 10–12 hour overnight fast.
